summary: The Christmas tree footprint calculator takes the numbers you enter and reports the entire tree adsorbed (Hidden variables & tree data) immediately. It is free to use, needs no account, and shows the working rather than just the answer. It suits a footprint, a resource or an environmental change you want to size up. Every field is labelled the way you would say it out loud, so you can usually fill the form from memory and only look up the numbers you genuinely do not know.

sections.title: How does the Christmas tree footprint calculator work?
sections.html:
The Christmas tree footprint calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports the entire tree adsorbed (Hidden variables & tree data) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the tree size (Current Christmas tree footprint), the delivery location (Current Christmas tree footprint) and your engine type (Current Christmas tree footprint)); then you type in the tree's source to shop (Current Christmas tree footprint), how far? (Current Christmas tree footprint), the distance to end point? (Current Christmas tree footprint) and the tree's source to shop (Other Christmas tree options).

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Christmas tree footprint calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

The entire tree adsorbed=(13149 ÷ 16) × How tall is your tree? × My engine produces adsorbed over area × (How wide is your tree? ^ 2) ÷ yearly growth
My engine produces=c o2 diesel × your engine type − c o2 petrol × your engine type + c o2 petrol
Your current tree produces=(how will you pick up your tree?, how far?, my engine produces, my tree will end up..., tree's source to shop, the entire tree adsorbed, distance to end point?)
Your current tree produces=(how will you pick up your tree?, how far?, my engine produces, How heavy is your tree?, distance to end point?, next year, where did your tree come from?, distance over the ocean, distance via train)
Co 2 adsorbed over area=(16 ÷ 13149) × the entire tree adsorbed × yearly growth ÷ (How tall is your tree? × (How wide is your tree? ^ 2))
Your engine type=(my engine produces − c o2 petrol2) ÷ (c o2 diesel2 − c o2 petrol2)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Length, opening in meters
  • Length, opening in meters
  • Mass, opening in kilograms
  • Length, opening in kilometers
  • Length, opening in miles
  • Length, opening in kilometers
  • Length, opening in kilometers
  • Length, opening in kilometers

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Christmas tree footprint calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Putting a headline figure into context
  • Sizing an environmental impact in familiar units
  • Comparing two options on the same basis
  • Any time the same 1 figures keep coming back — the tree's source to shop — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Christmas tree footprint calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns the entire tree adsorbed (Hidden variables & tree data), derived from the tree's source to shop. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Christmas tree footprint calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the tree's source to shop, which is 124 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter How tall is your tree? (Current Christmas tree footprint) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. How tall is your tree? (Current Christmas tree footprint) opens in meters and the chip beside it offers 34 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (113 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports How tall is your tree? = 0 m. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Christmas tree footprint calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
